title: SIU clears Brantford officer of wrongdoing after reopening two cases
subtitle: The province's police watchdog had reopened probes into the 2010 shooting of Evan Jones and 2009 drowning of Benjamin Wood in 2014, after an officer came forward with new information.
article: Brantford Police Const. Adam Hill walked into his force's headquarters at 4:45 a.m. on December 10, 2014. Unstable, dishevelled, and frenzied, he had an urgent need to talk - about how he had "lied" to the province's police watchdog. About how he was a "murderer."
What followed over two days were varying confessions to colleagues about his role in the deaths of Benjamin Wood and Evan Jones - young men killed during interactions with Brantford police.

Hill's utterances would set off a chain reaction, prompting the Special Investigations Unit, Ontario's civilian police watchdog, to take the exceedingly rare step of reopening two police-involved death investigations in 2015.

In a news release issued Monday, the SIU stated that after a comprehensive two-year re-investigation, no new charges will be laid in the deaths. Hill, the release said, was "in a state of medical distress" when he went to the police headquarters and claimed he was criminally responsible for both deaths.

The probe was significantly hampered by the failure of seven Brantford officers to video or audio record - or even take detailed notes - of Hill's statements. In Jones' case, the deficiencies in the officers' recording methods were "fatal" to SIU efforts, said the watchdog's director Tony Loparco.

"None of the officers at the police station made use of audio or video recording equipment that would have been available to them. While the four officers at the station did make notes, none of them attempted to record what the subject officer was saying word-for-word," writes SIU director Tony Loparco.

"In light of these inherent limitations, the only option left to the SIU in order to attempt to determine precisely what the subject officer said was to conduct witness officer interviews. The evidentiary value of statements obtained in this manner is dependent on the quality and accuracy of the witness' recall."

"After a thorough review of all of the available evidence, I have concluded that there are insufficient grounds to believe that a criminal offence has been committed in relation to the deaths of both Mr. Wood and Mr. Jones."

Monday's announcement is a disappointing end to a years-long saga, said Glenn Stuart, lawyer for Jones' family: "In effect it sounds as if there may have been the evidence to lay a charge if the Brantford Police Service had done their job."
"It's really quite amazing that someone could walk in to a police station and confess . . . and no one makes any record of that."

Monday's SIU release makes public for the first time that Hill was involved in Wood's and Jones' deaths. While the SIU does not name the subject officer involved in the case, he was identified in Jones' coroner's inquest and the Star and other media have previously published his name.

Earlier SIU probes cleared Hill in the deaths, but the investigations into their deaths were "immediately" reopened "given the enormity of" Hill's claims to fellow officers in varying utterances to officers in December 2014 that he was criminally responsible in the men's deaths. In his varying utterances to officers, he claimed he shot and killed an unarmed Jones, that he had struck Wood in the head in a "heavy handed way" he'd never before revealed, that he had "lied" to the SIU, and more.

Monday's SIU release sheds light on a high-stakes reinvestigation by the watchdog that hinged on Hill's mental state during his comments to police, and forced the watchdog to retain a forensic psychiatrist to provide an expert opinion about Hill's statements and obtain three production orders related to the officer's mental health.

The SIU interviewed 10 police witnesses; Hill did not participate in the reinvestigations, as is his legal right. Loparco found Hill "was disjointed, and characterized by religious and paranoid delusions." Hours after he walked into the police station, Hill was admitted to a health-care facility, the release states.

The Brantford Police Service did not respond to the Star's questions about why Hill's colleagues failed to record or write down his comments, and why it took eight days to alert the SIU about Hill's comments. But in a statement posted on the BPS website Monday, the force said a review of policy "relevant to the two incidents will be undertaken" and results brought to Brantford's police board in 30 days.

"Today is a particularly difficult day for those who are revisiting emotions connected to these incidents and the loss of Mr. Wood and Mr. Jones. Our thoughts are with all those affected," Chief Geoff Nelson said in a statement.
Due to an ongoing civil suit by Jones' family, the service said it would not be providing further comment.

Brantford Police Association president Mark Baxter told the Star that Loparco's criticism of officers for failing to record Hill's comments was is an "extraordinary after-the-fact assumption" and "Monday morning quarterbacking."

"Virtually everything (Hill) said that night was wrong," Baxter said, adding that the officers dealt with Hill compassionately. In particular, some of the officers were visiting Hill while he was in hospital two days later could not have been expected to take notes or record."

Wood, 32, died from drowning and hypothermia on Jan. 20, 2009. Police had pursued him to the edge of the frozen Grand River following his escape from a stolen vehicle. After a struggle with Hill, Wood went further out and broke the ice, falling into the river and prompting an hours-long search for his body. A coroner's inquest was not called to examine Wood's death.

In his comments about Wood's death, Hill told colleagues he hit Wood on the head a number of times during the altercation and in a way that he described as "heavy handed." He told one officer he did not tell the SIU about that because "he was scared" and said that after he hit Wood on the head, the man broke free and ran out on the ice.
"He opined that Mr. Wood did not return to the shoreline because he had been struck by (Hill)," read the SIU release.

However, Loparco explains that Hill's claims would not result in charges because they were "flatly contradicted" by other evidence. Two witnesses said Hill did not strike Wood before Wood ran away, and a post-mortem found no evidence of his being struck on the head.
Jones, 18, died at home on Aug. 25, 2010. His mother had called 911 because he was upset, yelling and throwing furniture; he struggled with depression, substance abuse and suicidal thoughts.

Police found Jones holding a butcher knife and a meat cleaver. He told police to shoot him, then threw a knife toward Hill. The SIU initially cleared Hill because he believed an officer was in imminent danger.

The reinvestigation into Hill's comments about Jones' death was more complex. Then in his December 2014 comments, Hill gave varying accounts of the incident, saying both that he "shot an unarmed man" and he was unsure whether Jones was armed when he fired but "was relieved to see a meat cleaver near his body after the fact."

He also claimed that a Brantford Police Association representative counselled him to lie to the SIU in the 2010 investigation, and that the representative told him to say that Jones was holding the knife above his head, not 90 degrees from his body. The SIU release states that the unnamed representative categorically denied counselling the subject officer to lie. Baxter told the Star Monday that the BPA "has never and would never counsel any member to break the law."

Loparco said that in addition to the problems due to the failure of the officers to record Hill's statements, the content of Hill's comments were "inherently unreliable," noting that Hill told one officer there was no knife at all, then the next that he had been counselled to lie about its position."

"The statements that the SIU was able to obtain in the circumstances cannot satisfy the evidentiary threshold for admissibility. They can only be viewed as inaccurate, unreliable and incomplete . . . Given that these statements lack the necessary features to even attempt admitting them into evidence, there is no basis to interfere with the previous conclusion that the shooting of Mr. Jones was legally justified."

Prior to Wood's and Jones' death, Hill was also involved in another fatal police interaction. In 2006, he was one of two officers involved in the fatal shooting of Andrew Osidacz, a man who had just killed his son and was holding a woman hostage with a knife. No charge was laid against Hill or his fellow officer in that case.

In 2012, Jones' family filed a lawsuit against Hill, the Brantford Police Services Board, retired police chief Derek McElveny, and Hill's fellow officers alleging negligence and assault and battery, among other things.
The suit alleges that after the 2006 shooting involving Hill, the officer returned to duty without a full psychiatric assessment or treatment.

"As a result, no proper determination was made . . . as to whether the trauma of this earlier incident impacted his ability to exercise his judgment required in his future duties as a police officer," the Jones family alleges in the suit.

A statement of defence filed in January 2013 did not directly address allegations Hill was not properly treated following his first shooting, though it did state that "unless otherwise admitted, the defendants deny or have no knowledge of the allegations contained" in the suit.
Stuart, the Jones family lawyer, said the civil suit can now resume and they will explore whether there are "further grounds for liability."
